idiom_name: props-only component typed by an interface; supply half is a typed custom hook (or a typed container component)
implementation_notes: TypeScript adds no mechanism - the split is the same props-in, data-out arrangement - but the types become the contract: the presentational component's props interface states exactly what the view needs, the supply hook returns exactly that shape, and the compiler rejects a view that reaches for a store it was not handed, as long as the store is typed rather than ambient. Keep the props interface exhaustive (no optional or widened fields) and readonly where possible so tests and stories can build it from a literal. The classic container remains for connect()-generated components and error boundaries, and typed DI frameworks such as Angular realize the same split with services instead of hooks.
pitfalls: A props interface with optional or widened fields lets callers omit data the view needs; keep it exhaustive and readonly.
A hook that returns a fresh object on every render re-renders every child; memoise the returned callbacks or split the hook.
Module-level stores or untyped context make the supply half unreplaceable in tests; inject it through props, a typed context or a hook parameter.

variants.name: Typed container generated by connect()
variants.idiom_name: typed higher-order component injecting a typed state-props subset
variants.implementation_notes: The generated container again, now typed: connect()/withRouter-style wrappers inject data and callbacks as props and the presentational component underneath is unchanged. Keep the mapper's return type explicit (a typed subset of the view's props), otherwise inference widens and the view loses the guarantee that it renders only what it was given. This form is worth keeping where the data source itself must be exchanged per screen and the higher-order component is the seam that expresses that; prefer the hook variant for new code.
pitfalls: Wrappers stacked from several higher-order components make prop provenance untraceable and collapse type inference; flatten them or move to hooks.
A mapper that returns a new object on every store change re-renders the presentational view constantly; memoise the selectors.
Loose generics on the wrapper (any, Record<string, unknown>) erase the guarantee that the view renders only what it was given.

variants.name: Angular: smart component with injected service, dumb components with @Input/@Output
variants.idiom_name: smart (container) component injecting the data service; presentational components with @Input bindings and @Output events
variants.implementation_notes: Angular's architecture separates the halves by type: a component presents properties and methods for data binding, while services hold the business logic and the data access and are handed to the smart component through dependency injection. The smart component injects the service, owns loading and error state and passes values down through @Input bindings, while the presentational component declares only its inputs and emits @Output events - it never injects the data service. Keep HTTP calls in the service, and use OnPush change detection on the presentational components so their rendering depends only on their inputs.
pitfalls: An @Input mutated inside the child breaks one-way flow; emit an @Output event instead.
Injecting the data service into a presentational component makes it a smart component with a dumb name; keep services out of the leaf.
Without OnPush change detection the leaf re-renders on every parent cycle, so the split stops buying anything.
